subject: Anatomy
summary: Metacarpals are the five long bones of the hand that form the palm skeleton and transmit forces from the fingers to the wrist. Their shape, articulations and blood supply are crucial for grip, fine motor tasks and for recognizing trauma patterns.

sections.p: The metacarpals are numbered 1‑5 from thumb to little finger. Each has a shaft, a base that articulates with the carpal row, and a head that forms the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint.
b: Thumb metacarpal is shorter and more mobile
Fifth metacarpal has a styloid process for muscle attachment

sections.p: They lie in the palm between the carpal bones proximally and the proximal phalanges distally. The base is broad, the shaft is cylindrical, and the head is rounded for hinge‑like MCP joints.
b: Base articulates with trapezium (1st) to hamate (5th)
Shaft contains a central medullary canal
Head forms a condylar surface for finger flexion/extension

sections.p: Deep to the metacarpals run the interosseous muscles, palmar arches, and digital nerves. Laterally, the extensor tendons cross over the dorsal surface.
b: Palmar metacarpal arteries arise from deep palmar arch
Ulnar nerve supplies the medial three digits
Radial nerve supplies the thumb and index

sections.p: Each metacarpal receives blood from the palmar metacarpal arteries (branches of the deep palmar arch) and dorsal metacarpal arteries (branches of the dorsal carpal arch).
b: Head receives branches from digital arteries

sections.p: Sensory innervation follows the digital nerves: radial nerve to the thumb and index, ulnar nerve to the ring and little fingers; the median nerve supplies the lateral three and a half digits on the palmar side.
b: Motor supply to interossei and lumbricals via ulnar and median nerves

sections.p: Metacarpals act as levers for finger motion, transmit grip forces, and allow opposition of the thumb through the first metacarpal‑trapezium joint.
Fractures, congenital shortening, and metabolic bone disease affect the metacarpals. Recognising patterns guides imaging, management and prognosis.
b: Boxer’s fracture – transverse fracture of the 5th metacarpal neck
Metacarpal shortening in Albright hereditary osteodystrophy
Osteolytic lesions (e.g., tuberculous osteomyelitis) may mimic cysts

t.b: Confirms fracture type, displacement and involvement of MCP joint; if unavailable, clinical alignment and neurovascular exam guide urgent referral
Evaluates metabolic bone disease such as Albright hereditary osteodystrophy; if labs unavailable, look for clinical triad (short stature, round face, short 4th metacarpal)
Detects occult fractures, bone marrow edema, or infection when X‑ray is normal; if MRI not feasible, treat based on clinical suspicion and immobilisation

sections.p: Inspection for shortening, deformity, or swelling; palpate each metacarpal shaft and MCP joints; assess range of motion and neurovascular status.
b: Loss of thumb opposition suggests first metacarpal‑trapezium pathology
Tenderness over the 5th metacarpal neck indicates a boxer’s fracture

whenToSeekHelp: Severe crush injury with loss of sensation distal to the wrist

faq.q: Why does a short 4th metacarpal suggest Albright hereditary osteodystrophy?
faq.a: It reflects abnormal bone remodeling due to PTH resistance, a hallmark of the disorder.

faq.q: What is the typical management of a non‑displaced 5th metacarpal neck fracture?
faq.a: Buddy taping or a splint for 3‑4 weeks, with early finger motion to prevent stiffness.

faq.q: Can a metacarpal infection occur without an obvious wound?
faq.a: Yes, hematogenous spread from TB or HIV‑related opportunistic infections can produce osteomyelitis.

exam: Describe the articulations of the first metacarpal and their relevance to thumb opposition.
Explain how to differentiate a boxer’s fracture from a simple soft‑tissue injury on examination.
List the blood supply to the metacarpals and why it matters in fracture healing.
